deep.reconstruction:
The page is drawn on the back of a recycled IBM/JES2 printer banner sheet. The printout reads '//* CRAY2 0411', four large block slashed zeros, block letters 'CRAY2', and the end-of-job lines dated 16 Aug 82. The printout has no mathematical content; it only shows Grothendieck was using scrap computer paper. All the mathematics is in the coloured drawings, which carry no words.

The drawings belong to his 1983-84 study of 'systèmes de pseudo-droites': arrangements of pseudolines, viewed in the projective plane or in a disc model.

(1) Two large discs. Each holds an arrangement of orange/brown pseudo-line arcs running from boundary to boundary.
- Arcs of the boundary circle are emphasised in dark green or black, with green or black marked points on the circle. These are likely the 'bouts marqués' (marked ends) of the previous page.
- Some cells are hatched yellow or orange. They are mostly triangular cells and cells next to the boundary or to the marked arcs.
- In the left disc, dashed and dotted black/green curves trace paths through the arrangement. These are plausibly the 'canaux' (channels), i.e. the 'lieu des cours entre bouts marqués' (locus of courses between marked ends) of the previous page.
- The black squiggles on the right boundary of both discs may mark the 'étoiles exceptionnelles' (exceptional stars), i.e. multiple points or local modifications at the boundary.
- The hatched triangles suggest he is tracking triangular cells, the loci of elementary mutations (triangle flips), and how they sit relative to the marked boundary data.

(2) Top right: a green line crossed obliquely by an orange line, with two short orange transversals. Separately there is a green X. These are elementary local crossing configurations: a crossing, and how other lines cut a pair of crossing lines.

(3) Bottom right: a horizontal strip divided by vertical green lines into fundamental domains, with a horizontal green/black central line. Orange curves form repeated lens-shaped and bundle patterns above and below it.
- This reads as a periodic, wiring-diagram-like picture: an arrangement cut open along a line, or the lift to the universal cover of the Möbius band obtained from the projective plane minus a point.
- On that cover, one distinguished pseudoline becomes the axis and the others become periodic curves.
- The next page continues with 'bundles of red curves between vertical green lines above and below a horizontal green line' and with level labels 0,1,2,3. That supports the reading that he is counting levels or crossing numbers of curves relative to a reference line, in a periodic strip.

Overall, the page is exploratory visual case-work on the combinatorics of pseudoline arrangements: cells, triangles, boundary marking, channels, and periodic strip models. It states no result.
